summary: Initial economic intake to understand which hosting mode makes sense for Delphi's document summarization product. Key constraints: monthly budget cap (~$12k), sub-200ms tail latency target for user-facing calls, data residency in us-west, requirement for audit logs and KMS. Discussed per-token levers (batching, prefix/KV cache, quantization), Dedicated reserved vs Hosted bursts, and quick pilot plan to validate unit economics.
topics: batching and cache benefits and latency tradeoffs
Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private (VPC) fit
security: KMS, audit logs, SOC2 evidence
transcript: 00:00 Priya (Redwood AE): okay hi everyone thanks for joining, i'm Priya from Redwood. we have luis and jared joining from the solutions team. who do we have on the Delphi side?
00:08 Maya (Delphi): hey priya, maya here. tom and aisha with me. we pulled in our security lead, they're on but might be on mute - they'll chime in for compliance questions.

00:16 Priya: excellent, goal for today is to map your budget and latency constraints to hosting options and show which levers move unit cost. quick confirm - you mentioned a monthly budget cap around 12k?
00:26 Aisha (CTO): yeah rough target is under 12k to start for the pilot. if costs scale predictably we can expand but we need predictable unit economics first.
00:33 Luis (Redwood SE): okay cool — can you share expected qps and average prompt lengths so we can ballpark tokens?

00:40 Tom (Platform): we're looking at 600 - 1,200 user requests per day initially, but peaks at about 30 concurrent in product spikes. average prompt+completion is around 280 tokens total, with a 75 token user prompt and 205 token model response on average.

00:58 Priya: got it. so using that rough traffic the important levers are batching at the runtime, prefix caching for repeated context, and quantization choices. batching reduces per-token overhead but it can add tail latency if you wait for batch fill — that's the classic tradeoff.
01:16 Maya: can you say more about prefix or kv cache? we do a lot of doc summarization where the beginning of the doc is repeated across calls for the same user flow.

01:25 Luis: sure — our runtime supports prefix or kv caching where common context vectors or earlier tokens are kept in GPU memory (the kv cache). that avoids re-computing attention keys for repeated prefixes. it's great for throughput and cost because you only send delta tokens. caveat: if your working set is too large the cache evicts, so hit rates matter.
01:46 Tom: how do you measure hit rate? is there an easy way for us to know if our workload benefits?

01:51 Jared (Redwood): we have dashboard metrics in the console showing cache hit/miss ratios and token-level cost breakdown per route. for pilots we can instrument a short run to estimate hit rates from your sample prompts.
02:03 Maya: perfect. our main worry is latency — we want sub-200ms p95 for quick summaries. will batching break that?

02:10 Luis: batching can be tuned aggressively for latency-sensitive routes. continuous batching with small max waits (e.g., 5-10ms) still gives some benefits without exceeding tight latency SLOs. for p95 200ms it's doable with hosted low-latency instances or Dedicated with reserved pools to avoid noisy neighbors.
02:26 Aisha: what's the delta in unit cost between Hosted and Dedicated generally? ballpark numbers are fine.

02:33 Priya: ballpark — hosted is simplest but can be ~20-40% higher per-token because we include multi-tenant overhead and flex capacity. Dedicated reserved gives better unit economics, especially when you have sustained throughput, because you're amortizing GPU costs. we'll put concrete numbers in the spreadsheet but for your volumes, a small Dedicated pool may already be cost-competitive if you commit monthly.
02:52 Tom: our initial volume seems small — would a hosted pilot be cheaper to start and then switch to Dedicated?

02:58 Luis: yep that's a common path — start Hosted for speed of launch, measure token mix and cache hit rate, then move to Dedicated if steady. Redwood supports pinning model versions and rollout policies so transition is smoother. only caveat is data residency / VPC needs — if you need private networking from day one, Private/VPC deploy is recommended.
03:16 Speaker 1 (security): quick question on KMS and audit logs — do you integrate with customer KMS, and can we keep key material in our own HSM?

03:24 Jared: yes we integrate with common KMS providers and we support customer-managed keys/HSM for Private deployments. for Hosted we have an encrypted-at-rest model and we can provide SOC2 artifacts; for full HSM control you'd likely evaluate Private with our on-prem package.
03:39 Maya: okay good. on-cost modeling, you mentioned quantization — we have concerns about output quality with aggressive int8 quantization. how do you recommend balancing that?

03:47 Luis: right — quantization reduces memory footprint and increases throughput. we recommend trying 4-bit/8-bit profiles on non-critical routes first and validating outputs against your eval set. Redwood Optimize can suggest a quantization profile based on your prompts and quality thresholds.
03:59 Tom: is quantization automatic or manual? we don't want regressions in summary quality.

04:04 Priya: it's advisory — we never auto-apply in production without sign-off. Optimize will flag expected unit-cost gains and potential quality delta; we can run A/B tests in canary rollouts to validate.
04:14 Maya: what about fallback policies? if the Dedicated pool is saturated do you route to hosted or a smaller model?

04:20 Luis: we have smart routing — you can define policy-based fallbacks: route to Hosted, a lower-cost quantized variant, or a longer-latency cheaper tier. important to define which routes get priority; that keeps your surface available during spikes.
04:33 Aisha: sounds helpful. our legal team will want data residency and auditability. can you provide sample audit logs and retention options?
04:40 Jared: yes — we export tenancy-level audit logs, per-request traces, and token-level cost breakdowns. retention and export options are configurable, we can share the docs and an example export.
04:50 Maya: going back to cost math: for our 1k req/day at 280 tokens avg, do you have a quick calc on monthly token count and ballpark cost for hosted?

05:00 Priya: rough calc: 1k * 280 * 30 = 8.4M tokens/month. multiply by per-token pricing. for hosted baseline let's say $0.000012/token for generation (example), that'd be about $100/month — but that's a toy number; actual per-token includes context and possible prompt-cost multipliers. we'll run exact sims in spreadsheet.
05:18 Tom: those per-token numbers seem low compared to other vendors. is that including all overhead?

05:22 Priya: correct, it's illustrative. Redwood bills by effective token units and shows line items for model compute, routing, and storage. we also include options like reserved throughput which shifts into committed monthly fees but reduces per-token compute fees.
05:35 Maya: can we do a micro-benchmark on a representative sample? we want to see real token breakdown and cache benefits.
05:40 Luis: yes — we'll run a micro-benchmark using your sample prompts. ideal: you share 200-500 representative prompts (de-identified) so we can simulate cache hit patterns and batching behavior.
05:49 Maya: we can do that. security team: will we need an NDA to share prompts?
05:53 Speaker 1 (security): depends on data sensitivity; NDA preferred but we can first share de-identified redacted prompts. we want to avoid raw PII leaving our environment.
06:01 Priya: understood — we'll accept redacted inputs for the bench. Luis, could you outline what metrics you'll return?
06:07 Luis: we'll provide tokens per call, cache hit ratio, average latency and p95, GPU utilization, and per-token cost breakdown across variants (hosted, dedicated small pool, quantized model).
06:17 Tom: what's the expected timeline for the bench?
06:20 Luis: 7-10 business days after we get prompts and API access or sample harness. i'll target 6 business days, share results in a spreadsheet and a short findings call.
06:29 Maya: great. one more question — for dedicated pools, what do commit terms look like? monthly? annual?

06:34 Priya: we have monthly reserved capacity and annual commitments that offer deeper discounts. for pilots teams often do 1-month reserved or use burst capacity options so you're not overcommitting.
06:43 Aisha: and if we need VPC from day one?

06:46 Priya: Private/VPC is available but onboarding takes longer — you'd need networking steps, security reviews, and likely an enterprise contract. we can discuss a fast-path pilot with hosted plus strict data handling if that helps accelerate initial validation.
06:56 Maya: that could work, yes. any common gotchas you've seen with customers that start hosted then move to Dedicated?

07:02 Jared: watch for tokenization variance between models and test sets — often folks assume exact token counts but small prompt changes matter. also monitor cache working set and eviction policies; some teams get surprise costs when cache hit rate is lower than assumed.
07:16 Tom: okay noted. what about monitoring and cost alerts? can we set per-route alerts when spend exceeds threshold?
07:22 Priya: yes our console supports per-route budget alerts and token-level cost breakdown. we can also provide CSV exports for ingest into your billing pipeline.

07:29 Maya: let's recap — deliverables are pricing spreadsheet, bench results, security docs. timeline: pricing by april 2, bench results by april 6, customer to send prompts by april 1. does that capture it?
07:39 Aisha: yes that works for us, we'll aim to send redacted prompts by apr 1.
07:42 Priya: perfect. any final questions?
07:46 Speaker 1 (security): one last thing — retention policy. can you hold request logs for 90 days with exportable audit?
07:51 Jared: yes 90 days is standard for hosted; we can discuss extended retention in enterprise plans and export hooks for SIEMs.
07:59 Maya: thanks everyone. we'll wait for the spreadsheet and the bench plan. appreciate the clear path.
08:05 Priya: thanks all, we'll follow up with next steps and action items. bye.
